content: 1. Moderate-quality evidence suggests that increasing potassium intake to at least 90 mmol/day in adults is beneficial for reducing blood pressure, with no indication of adverse effects in children. However, high-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to determine the optimal level of potassium intake for maximizing health benefits are lacking, and further research is needed to clarify the precise target intake. 2. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are the leading cause of mortality globally, affecting countries across all regions and income levels. Interventions aimed at reducing the burden of NCDs are valuable and applicable in all contexts. 3. High-quality evidence supports the benefit of increased potassium intake in lowering blood pressure in adults. Blood pressure serves as a reliable proxy indicator for the risk of cardiovascular diseases, including stroke and coronary heart disease. 4. Although evidence from meta-analyses of cohort studies measuring cardiovascular disease or coronary heart disease outcomes is inconclusive, there is some indication that increased potassium intake may provide benefits. Cohort data specifically support the beneficial effect of increased potassium intake on reducing the risk of stroke. 5. Moderate-quality indirect evidence suggests that increasing potassium intake in children may have a positive effect on blood pressure. Additionally, high-quality evidence indicates that increased potassium intake in adults does not harm blood lipids, catecholamine levels, or renal function. No evidence of harm has been observed in children. 6. Achieving recommended potassium intake levels is feasible through the consumption of reasonable amounts of potassium-rich foods such as fresh fruits, vegetables, beans, dairy products, and other potassium-containing foods. Implementing this intervention requires consumer education, public health communications, and nutrition campaigns. 7. Reducing the burden of NCDs is highly cost-effective. These recommendations can be integrated into existing public health nutrition education campaigns and other nutrition programs at global, regional, national, and subnational levels. 8. The management of conflicts of interest was carefully addressed during the development of the WHO guidelines on potassium intake. Members of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health, including Professors John Cummings, Shiriki Kumanyika, Este Vorster, Ibrahim Elmadfa, Nahla Hwalla, Mary L’Abbé, Jim Mann, Darius Mozaffarian, Murray Skeaff, and others, declared their interests. These declarations were reviewed, and it was determined that none of the declared interests constituted conflicts of interest for their roles in the subgroup or the work being undertaken. 9. External experts and resource persons, such as Professors Francesco Cappuccio, Paul Elliott, and Paula Moynihan, also declared their interests. These individuals contributed to discussions of evidence but did not vote on the recommendations formulated during the NUGAG meetings. Their declared interests were documented, and no conflicts of interest were identified. 10. The guidelines emphasize the importance of transparency and appropriate disclosure of interests to ensure the integrity of the recommendations. All members and external experts involved in the process were required to submit signed declarations of interest forms.
